requirements.product_understanding: A rate-limiting system that enforces configurable request quotas (requests-per-minute) for each tenant on a multi-tenant API platform, distributed across many stateless API gateway nodes. The system allows per-endpoint override limits while maintaining consistent enforcement and avoiding single points of failure.
users_and_use_cases: Platform tenants: Configure their own requests-per-minute quota for their API usage
Platform tenants: Override default rate limits for specific API endpoints they consume
Platform ops: Monitor overall system rate-limiting performance and compliance
Platform ops: Ensure the rate-limiting system maintains 99.99% availability while handling 500,000 requests/sec across thousands of tenants
functional: Enforce configurable requests-per-minute quota per tenant
Support per-endpoint override limits for tenants
Distribute rate-limit decisions across multiple stateless API gateway nodes
Maintain consistent rate-limit enforcement across all gateway nodes
Allow tenants to configure their own quota limits
Enable tenants to set endpoint-specific override limits
non_functional: System must handle 500,000 requests/sec across all tenants
Rate-limit decision latency must be under 5ms p99
Total monthly cost must not exceed $15,000
System must not become single point of failure for the platform
assumptions: The system will use a distributed architecture approach to avoid single points of failure
API gateway nodes are stateless and can communicate with shared rate-limiting service
Tenant configuration data can be stored in a distributed cache or database
Rate-limit decisions can be made using counters that are periodically synchronized across nodes
The 500,000 requests/sec traffic is evenly distributed across thousands of tenants
Platform ops will have access to monitoring and alerting systems for rate-limiting performance
open_questions: What specific technologies or infrastructure components will be used for the distributed rate-limiting system?
How will tenant configurations be synchronized across gateway nodes?
What is the expected distribution of requests per tenant to determine optimal scaling?
What are the specific requirements for monitoring and alerting of rate-limiting performance?
How will endpoint override limits be validated and enforced consistently across all nodes?
What is the expected data model for storing tenant quota configurations and endpoint overrides?

components.name: RateLimitingEngine
components.description: Distributed rate-limiting engine that makes real-time decisions using atomic counters for all rate-limit checks to ensure consistent enforcement under high load. Processes requests from API gateways, checks tenant quotas and endpoint overrides, and enforces limits with strong consistency across all nodes. Operates as a stateless service that communicates with shared storage for quota data and sliding window state tracking. Scales horizontally by distributing tenants using fixed consistent hashing with virtual nodes to prevent hotspots. Uses lock-free atomic operations (compare-and-swap) for counter updates to maintain sub-5ms p99 latency under 500K requests/sec throughput.

components.name: TenantConfigStore
components.description: Distributed key-value store for tenant configuration data including default quotas and endpoint overrides. Stores all tenant-level rate-limit settings with TTL-based invalidation for stale configurations. Implements optimistic locking with retry logic for configuration updates to ensure consistency under high-frequency changes while maintaining low-latency performance. Scales horizontally by adding more nodes to the cluster and automatically redistributing tenant data using consistent hashing.

components.name: APIGateway
components.description: Stateless API gateway that forwards requests to backend services after rate-limiting checks. Makes individual POST calls to RateLimitingEngine's /rate-limit-check endpoint for each request with optimized HTTP/2 connection pooling for low-latency decision making. Does not maintain any rate-limiting state locally and relies entirely on distributed engine decisions. Handles request routing, authentication, and other gateway functions without impact from rate-limiting decisions. Processes requests at 500,000/sec throughput with minimal latency overhead from rate-limiting checks.

data_models.notes: Stores tenant-level rate-limiting configuration including default request limits and time windows.
Stores endpoint-specific override configurations for tenants. Each override applies to a specific API endpoint path within a tenant's scope.
Represents a sliding window counter for tracking request volume. Maintains count per tenant and endpoint within a specific time window to enforce rate limits.
Tracks state of each API gateway node including heartbeat information and tenant distribution for load balancing purposes.
Abstraction layer that maps tenant IDs to logical rate-limiting units for better decoupling of counter logic and configuration management.

apis.desc: Sets or updates tenant's default quota configuration with strict input validation and HMAC-signed request with timestamp and nonce
Updates tenant's default quota configuration with strict input validation and HMAC-signed request with timestamp and nonce
Creates endpoint-specific override limits for a tenant with strict input validation and HMAC-signed request with timestamp and nonce
Updates endpoint-specific override limit for a tenant with strict input validation and HMAC-signed request with timestamp and nonce
Removes endpoint-specific override limit for a tenant with HMAC-signed request with timestamp and nonce
Individual rate-limit check endpoint for each API gateway request with optimized HTTP/2 connection pooling

architecture.infrastructure: Distributed system using fixed consistent hashing with virtual nodes across multiple nodes. RateLimitingEngine instances use shared distributed cache for counters and TenantConfigStore for configuration data. APIGateway nodes are stateless with no local storage. All communication uses optimized HTTP/2 with connection pooling for low-latency decision making. Implements automatic failover between engine nodes with health checks every 100ms to maintain 99.99% availability target. Uses Redis cluster for distributed counters and configuration storage, with automatic sharding based on tenant ID hash. All components are deployed in Kubernetes clusters with horizontal autoscaling based on request volume metrics.

decisions.decision: Use atomic counters with lock-free operations for rate limiting
decisions.alternatives_considered: Probabilistic data structures (Count-Min Sketch), sliding window with atomic counters, fixed window, token bucket, leaky bucket algorithms
decisions.trade_offs: Atomic operations provide strong consistency but require more compute resources; probabilistic structures offer better scalability but introduce small false positive rates.
decisions.rationale: Required under 5ms p99 latency for rate-limit decisions. Atomic operations ensure correctness under 500K requests/sec load, eliminating the need for fallback validation on every request.

decisions.decision: Implement optimistic locking with retry logic for configuration updates
decisions.alternatives_considered: Queue-based system, optimistic locking with retry logic, pessimistic locking, single writer per tenant, distributed consensus protocols
decisions.trade_offs: Optimistic locking provides better performance under moderate load but may cause retries during high-concurrency scenarios.
decisions.rationale: Configuration updates are infrequent compared to request volume but could be substantial during peak usage. Optimistic locking with retry logic balances performance and consistency.

decisions.decision: Use fixed consistent hashing with virtual nodes for tenant distribution
decisions.alternatives_considered: Adaptive sharding based on load metrics, static consistent hashing, round-robin, random distribution, fixed sharding
decisions.trade_offs: Fixed consistent hashing provides better distribution and prevents hotspots but requires more complex node management; adaptive sharding is simpler but causes hotspots.
decisions.rationale: Required to avoid hotspots in high-traffic scenarios where tenant request volumes are unevenly distributed. Fixed consistent hashing with virtual nodes ensures efficient resource utilization without operational complexity.

decisions.decision: Use optimized HTTP/2 connection pooling for engine decisions
decisions.alternatives_considered: Persistent WebSocket connections, REST endpoints, gRPC streaming with buffering, message queues, event-driven architecture
decisions.trade_offs: HTTP/2 provides low-latency, efficient communication with connection pooling but requires careful management of concurrent connections.
decisions.rationale: Required to maintain under 5ms p99 rate-limit decision latency while avoiding the overhead of gRPC streaming that would exceed the latency budget.

decisions.decision: Implement circuit breaker and local caching for Redis unavailability
decisions.alternatives_considered: Simple retry logic, full failover, graceful degradation, complete service interruption
decisions.trade_offs: Circuit breaker adds complexity but provides better resilience; simple retry may cause cascading failures.
decisions.rationale: Ensures continued operation during Redis outages by allowing all requests through with warning logs and maintaining local cache for up to 5 minutes.

security_controls.threat_model_summary: Primary threats include tenant quota manipulation via API abuse, distributed denial-of-service through excessive configuration updates, counter race conditions during high-concurrency scenarios, potential cache invalidation delays causing false rate-limiting decisions, and unauthorized access if tenant API keys are compromised. Attackers may attempt to bypass rate limits by exploiting input validation weaknesses or by flooding the system with concurrent requests to trigger race conditions.
security_controls.authentication: APIGateway nodes authenticate with RateLimitingEngine using mTLS (mutual Transport Layer Security) with certificate-based identity verification. Tenant configuration APIs use HMAC-signed requests with tenant-specific secrets stored in Kubernetes Secrets, validated at the API gateway level before forwarding to RateLimitingEngine. Each request includes a valid HMAC-signed token or API key verified by the gateway to ensure only authorized tenants can influence rate-limit decisions. Timestamp validation within 5-minute window and unique nonces are enforced to prevent replay attacks.
security_controls.authorization: TenantConfigStore implements role-based access control where platform ops have full read/write permissions and tenants can only modify their own quota configurations via HMAC-protected endpoints. Endpoint override limits are validated against tenant ownership using a secure tenant ownership database (PostgreSQL) in addition to Redis lookup to ensure correctness even during cache invalidation events. All updates are performed within atomic transactions to maintain consistency.
security_controls.iam: Platform ops use service accounts with Kubernetes RBAC for cluster access, while tenants authenticate using API keys stored in Kubernetes Secrets and rotated automatically every 90 days. All IAM operations are audited through centralized log aggregation using Fluentd and Elasticsearch. Tenant API keys and HMAC secrets are rotated automatically every 90 days with centralized logging and auditing of access events. Key revocation list (KRL) is implemented to allow immediate invalidation of compromised keys without waiting for the next scheduled rotation.
security_controls.network_boundaries: APIGateway nodes operate in a public subnet with security groups allowing only HTTP/2 traffic from RateLimitingEngine instances, while RateLimitingEngine and TenantConfigStore run in private subnets with VPC peering for internal communication. All inter-component traffic uses mTLS with certificate rotation every 30 days. Connection limits and rate-limiting are enforced at the gateway level to prevent abuse of WebSocket connections. Service-to-service authentication between RateLimitingEngine instances uses mTLS with certificate-based identity verification.
security_controls.secrets_and_encryption: All secrets are stored in Kubernetes Secrets with encryption-at-rest using AES-256, rotated automatically every 90 days. API keys and HMAC signatures are encrypted in transit using TLS 1.3 with ephemeral key exchange. Sensitive data like tenant quotas is encrypted at rest using AWS KMS keys with automatic rotation every year, stored in Redis cluster with client-side encryption enabled for counter values. Encryption keys for Redis are rotated automatically to prevent exposure during node compromise.

reliability_design.scaling_strategy: The system scales horizontally using fixed consistent hashing with virtual nodes across RateLimitingEngine instances, with each engine handling a dynamic shard of tenants. APIGateway nodes are stateless and scale independently via Kubernetes autoscaling based on request volume metrics. The TenantConfigStore and RateLimitingEngine components use Redis cluster with automatic sharding to handle configuration and counter data distribution. Engine instances are scaled based on concurrent tenant processing needs, with each instance managing up to 10,000 tenants to maintain <5ms p99 latency target.
reliability_design.reliability: The system achieves 99.99% availability through: 1) Multi-instance RateLimitingEngine with automatic failover (health checks every 100ms), 2) Redis cluster with master-slave replication for TenantConfigStore and counter storage, 3) Stateless APIGateway nodes with no local storage, 4) Optimized HTTP/2 connection pooling from gateways to engines for real-time decision streaming, 5) Circuit breaker pattern in engine instances to detect Redis unavailability and gracefully degrade, 6) Local in-memory cache layer that temporarily stores tenant configurations during Redis outages.
reliability_design.disaster_recovery: For disaster recovery, the system implements: 1) Redis cluster with master-slave replication across availability zones, 2) Multi-region failover capability for RateLimitingEngine instances using Kubernetes deployment strategies, 3) Real-time replication of configuration changes to multiple Redis nodes with <1 minute RPO, 4) Hot standby Redis cluster with automatic failover within <30 seconds, 5) Data replication across multiple Redis nodes to prevent single points of failure in counter storage.
reliability_design.observability: The system includes: 1) Real-time metrics collection for rate-limit decisions (latency, throughput, success/failure rates), 2) Distributed tracing using OpenTelemetry for end-to-end request flow tracking, 3) Prometheus metrics exposed by all components with Grafana dashboards, 4) Alerting thresholds set at 5ms p99 latency and 0.01% error rate, 5) Centralized logging via ELK stack with structured logs from all services, 6) Dedicated Prometheus metrics to track atomic counter operations and detect anomalies such as failed atomic claims or counter increment failures.
failure_scenarios: RateLimitingEngine instance fails: Automatic failover within 100ms through health checks; Redis cluster maintains counter state; API gateways reconnect to new engine instance without interrupting service

TenantConfigStore Redis cluster node fails: Master-slave replication ensures no data loss; Engine instances continue processing with cached configurations until recovery; Configuration updates are retried once restored

RateLimitingEngine Redis cluster failure: Counter state is maintained in memory for 60 seconds (window size) to prevent immediate service disruption; System continues operating with eventual consistency model

APIGateway node loses connection to RateLimitingEngine: Optimized HTTP/2 connection pooling with automatic reconnection mechanism; Gateways cache recent tenant configurations for up to 1 minute during disconnection
High-concurrency race condition in counter increment: Lock-free atomic operations prevent contention; System handles over 500,000 requests/sec without counter corruption or enforcement errors
Tenant configuration update conflict: Optimistic locking with retry logic ensures consistency; No data loss or inconsistency during high-volume configuration changes
Redis unavailability: Circuit breaker pattern detects Redis failure and gracefully degrades by allowing all requests through with warning logs; Local cache maintains operations for up to 5 minutes

findings.issue: Tenant configuration APIs are protected only by HMAC-signed requests with timestamp and nonce, but lack rate-limiting on the configuration endpoints themselves. This creates a potential DoS vector where an attacker could flood these endpoints with configuration updates to exhaust resources or cause retries due to optimistic locking.
findings.recommendation: Implement rate-limiting on all tenant-facing configuration APIs (/tenants/{tenant_id}/quota, /tenants/{tenant_id}/overrides) with a low quota (e.g., 10 requests/minute per tenant) to prevent abuse. This should be enforced before HMAC validation to avoid wasting compute on invalid requests.

findings.issue: While mTLS is used between APIGateway and RateLimitingEngine, there's no indication of how tenant identity is propagated from the gateway to the engine. If tenants are not authenticated at the gateway level before forwarding to the engine, the engine cannot verify which tenant is making a request.
findings.recommendation: Ensure that APIGateway nodes authenticate each incoming request with tenant credentials (e.g., API key or JWT) and propagate tenant identity via headers to RateLimitingEngine. The engine must validate this tenant identity against the HMAC signature for configuration updates, and use it for rate-limit decisions.

findings.issue: Authorization is enforced using a secure tenant ownership database (PostgreSQL) in addition to Redis lookup, but there's no mention of how access control is enforced within the RateLimitingEngine itself. If an attacker can bypass the gateway or forge requests, they may be able to make unauthorized rate-limit decisions.
findings.recommendation: Implement strict authorization checks inside the RateLimitingEngine that validate tenant ownership and endpoint override permissions directly against the PostgreSQL-backed tenant ownership database, even when a request comes from an authenticated gateway node. This prevents escalation of privileges if the gateway is compromised.

findings.issue: The system uses mTLS for internal communication but doesn't specify how Redis cluster nodes are secured. If Redis is accessible from untrusted networks or lacks proper access controls, an attacker could gain read/write access to tenant quotas and counters.
findings.recommendation: Ensure Redis clusters are deployed in private subnets with strict VPC security groups that allow only internal traffic from RateLimitingEngine instances. Implement Redis ACLs or use Redis with built-in authentication mechanisms, and rotate Redis credentials regularly.

findings.issue: Tenant API keys are stored in Kubernetes Secrets and rotated every 90 days, but there's no mention of how these secrets are used for HMAC signing. If the same key is reused across multiple tenants or if the HMAC algorithm is weak (e.g., SHA-1), it could be vulnerable to collision attacks.
findings.recommendation: Use a strong HMAC algorithm like SHA-256 or SHA-3, and ensure that each tenant has a unique HMAC secret. Additionally, consider using per-request nonce generation with time-based validity windows (e.g., 5-minute TTL) to prevent replay attacks.

findings.issue: The primary cost drivers are Redis cluster instances for distributed counters and configuration storage, plus Kubernetes cluster management. The architecture uses Redis cluster with master-slave replication across availability zones, which is expensive but necessary for the required 99.99% availability and strong consistency.
findings.recommendation: Monitor Redis memory usage closely to prevent unexpected scaling costs; consider using Redis Enterprise Edition for better performance and cost efficiency.

findings.issue: The system assumes 500,000 requests/sec across thousands of tenants with atomic counters. While the design uses lock-free operations, this scale may strain Redis cluster performance under peak loads, especially if tenant request volumes are unevenly distributed.
findings.recommendation: Implement additional monitoring for Redis latency and throughput; consider sharding strategies or caching layers to reduce direct Redis load during traffic spikes.

findings.issue: The budget of $15,000/month is sufficient for the current architecture but leaves little room for unexpected traffic spikes or additional features like advanced analytics or enhanced monitoring. The system's cost estimate is at the upper end of the budget range.
findings.recommendation: Plan for a 20-30% buffer in the budget to accommodate potential scaling needs or feature additions without exceeding financial limits.

findings.issue: The system's 99.99% availability target is not fully supported by the proposed architecture. The reliance on Redis cluster for counter storage and configuration with a 60-second in-memory cache fallback during Redis unavailability introduces a potential single point of failure (SPOF) if the Redis cluster fails and recovery takes longer than 60 seconds, or if multiple Redis nodes fail simultaneously.
findings.recommendation: Implement a multi-tiered caching strategy with a distributed consensus-based counter system (e.g., using etcd or similar) as a backup to Redis for critical counter data. This ensures that even during extended Redis outages, rate-limiting decisions can be made with minimal disruption and maintain the required 99.99% availability target.

findings.issue: The disaster recovery strategy specifies a <1 minute RPO for configuration changes, but does not clearly define how this is enforced in practice. The system's reliance on Redis master-slave replication and caching mechanisms may not guarantee atomicity of all configuration updates, potentially leading to inconsistencies or data loss in the event of a failure.
findings.recommendation: Implement a write-ahead log (WAL) for all tenant configuration changes with strict consistency guarantees. Ensure that all configuration updates are durably stored before being acknowledged to prevent data loss during failures and meet the <1 minute RPO requirement.

findings.issue: The architecture does not adequately address potential race conditions or inconsistencies in counter updates when multiple API gateways attempt to increment counters simultaneously. While atomic operations are used, there is no explicit mechanism to handle scenarios where the Redis cluster becomes unavailable during a counter update, potentially leading to incorrect rate-limiting decisions.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a circuit breaker pattern with a configurable timeout for Redis operations and implement a fallback mechanism that allows requests to proceed with a warning log when Redis is unavailable. Additionally, add a secondary validation step in the RateLimitingEngine to detect and correct any inconsistencies in counter values after recovery from an outage.

findings.issue: The observability strategy includes metrics collection and tracing but lacks specific monitoring for atomic counter operations and anomaly detection. This could lead to undetected issues such as failed atomic claims or counter increment failures that might affect rate-limiting accuracy.
findings.recommendation: Add dedicated Prometheus metrics specifically for tracking atomic counter operations, including failure rates, latency distributions, and anomalies in counter updates. Implement alerting thresholds for these metrics to proactively detect issues with the rate-limiting engine's core functionality.

findings.issue: The architecture uses a REST POST endpoint (/rate-limit-check) for every single request, which is fundamentally incompatible with the stated requirement of 500,000 requests/sec throughput and under 5ms p99 latency. This approach creates a massive network overhead and serialization bottleneck at the gateway level.
findings.recommendation: Replace individual REST POST calls with a streaming gRPC interface or WebSocket connection per API gateway node to reduce per-request overhead and enable more efficient batching of rate-limit decisions.

findings.issue: The RateLimitingEngine is tightly coupled to Redis for both configuration and counter storage, creating a single point of failure in the distributed system. If Redis becomes unavailable, even temporarily, all rate-limiting decisions will fail or degrade.
findings.recommendation: Implement a multi-layered caching strategy where critical tenant configurations are cached locally on each engine instance with a secondary fallback to a redundant Redis cluster, and add a circuit breaker pattern that allows for graceful degradation when Redis is unreachable.

findings.issue: There's duplication between the 'RateLimitCounter' entity and the 'TenantQuota' entity in terms of storing window information. This redundancy increases storage overhead and complicates consistency management.
findings.recommendation: Refactor the data model to consolidate time window definitions into a single source of truth, eliminating redundant fields and simplifying update logic.

findings.issue: The assumption that 500K requests/sec can be handled with atomic counters on a single Redis cluster is flawed. Even with lock-free operations, the write volume to Redis will likely become a bottleneck at this scale.
findings.recommendation: Implement a hybrid approach where sliding window counters are maintained in memory on each engine node for short time windows (e.g., 10 seconds), and only aggregated periodically to Redis for consistency checks.

findings.issue: The system claims 99.99% availability but relies heavily on Redis clusters, which are not inherently fault-tolerant at the scale required. The architecture lacks sufficient redundancy in the counter storage layer.
findings.recommendation: Design a multi-region replication strategy for counter data with automatic failover capabilities, and implement a more resilient caching layer that can sustain Redis outages without compromising rate-limiting accuracy.

findings.issue: The security model includes both HMAC-signed requests and mTLS authentication, which introduces unnecessary complexity and potential points of failure. The same tenant ID could be used to bypass controls if not properly validated across layers.
findings.recommendation: Simplify the authentication flow by using only mTLS for service-to-service communication and HMAC validation at the API gateway level, ensuring that all tenant identity checks are centralized and consistent.

findings.issue: While observability is mentioned, there's no specific mention of how rate-limiting decisions will be audited or logged in a way that supports compliance or forensic analysis. This could be critical for platform operations.
findings.recommendation: Add structured logging and audit trails for all rate-limiting decisions, including timestamps, tenant IDs, endpoint paths, and whether the decision was to allow or deny the request.

architecture_stages.characteristics: A minimal, single-instance rate-limiting system that validates core functionality with a small subset of tenants. The system uses a centralized Redis instance for counters and configuration storage, with a simplified API gateway that makes direct calls to a single RateLimitingEngine instance. Tenant quotas are stored in a simple key-value store without endpoint overrides. The system handles 10K requests/sec across 100 tenants with basic monitoring and alerting.
architecture_stages.purpose: Validate the core rate-limiting concept and validate tenant configuration workflows with minimal infrastructure investment while maintaining the essential functionality of quota enforcement.
architecture_stages.transition_trigger: When the system reaches 10K requests/sec throughput or when cost exceeds $2,000/month due to inefficient resource usage.

architecture_stages.characteristics: The system scales horizontally with multiple RateLimitingEngine instances using consistent hashing for tenant distribution. The TenantConfigStore is upgraded to a Redis cluster with master-slave replication for high availability. APIGateway nodes maintain stateless operation but include local caching for tenant configurations to reduce latency. Endpoint override limits are supported, and the system handles 100K requests/sec across 1,000 tenants with enhanced monitoring, alerting, and circuit breaker patterns.
architecture_stages.purpose: Scale the system to support increasing traffic and tenant count while maintaining performance and reliability under moderate load conditions.
architecture_stages.transition_trigger: When the system reaches 100K requests/sec throughput or when latency exceeds 10ms p99 due to increased load on single engine instances.

architecture_stages.characteristics: The system implements regional distribution with separate RateLimitingEngine clusters per region, using a global configuration service for tenant data synchronization. Partitioning strategies are applied to counters and configurations across multiple Redis shards. Specialized services handle endpoint override validation and counter aggregation. The system supports 500K requests/sec across 10,000 tenants with full multi-region failover capabilities, advanced analytics, and machine learning-based anomaly detection for rate-limiting behavior.
architecture_stages.purpose: Support massive scale and global distribution while maintaining sub-5ms p99 latency, 99.99% availability, and cost efficiency under peak load conditions.
architecture_stages.transition_trigger: When the system reaches 500K requests/sec throughput or when Redis cluster becomes a bottleneck with >100ms p99 latency for counter operations.

If an attacker can bypass the gateway or forge requests, they may be able to make unauthorized rate-limit decisions.
threats.recommendation: Implement strict authorization checks inside the RateLimitingEngine that validate tenant ownership and endpoint override permissions directly against the PostgreSQL-backed tenant ownership database, even when a request comes from an authenticated gateway node. This prevents escalation of privileges if the gateway is compromised.

threats.issue: The system uses mTLS for internal communication but doesn't specify how Redis cluster nodes are secured. If Redis is accessible from untrusted networks or lacks proper access controls, an attacker could gain read/write access to tenant quotas and counters.
threats.recommendation: Ensure Redis clusters are deployed in private subnets with strict VPC security groups that allow only internal traffic from RateLimitingEngine instances. Implement Redis ACLs or use Redis with built-in authentication mechanisms, and rotate Redis credentials regularly.

threats.issue: Tenant API keys are stored in Kubernetes Secrets and rotated every 90 days, but there's no mention of how these secrets are used for HMAC signing. If the same key is reused across multiple tenants or if the HMAC algorithm is weak (e.g., SHA-1), it could be vulnerable to collision attacks.
threats.recommendation: Use a strong HMAC algorithm like SHA-256 or SHA-3, and ensure that each tenant has a unique HMAC secret. Additionally, consider using per-request nonce generation with time-based validity windows (e.g., 5-minute TTL) to prevent replay attacks.

blueprint.infrastructure: Distributed system using fixed consistent hashing with virtual nodes across multiple nodes. RateLimitingEngine instances use shared distributed cache for counters and TenantConfigStore for configuration data. APIGateway nodes are stateless with no local storage. All communication uses optimized HTTP/2 with connection pooling for low-latency decision making. Implements automatic failover between engine nodes with health checks every 100ms to maintain 99.99% availability target. Uses Redis cluster for distributed counters and configuration storage, with automatic sharding based on tenant ID hash. All components are deployed in Kubernetes clusters with horizontal autoscaling based on request volume metrics.
blueprint.scaling_strategy: The system scales horizontally using fixed consistent hashing with virtual nodes across RateLimitingEngine instances, with each engine handling a dynamic shard of tenants. APIGateway nodes are stateless and scale independently via Kubernetes autoscaling based on request volume metrics. The TenantConfigStore and RateLimitingEngine components use Redis cluster with automatic sharding to handle configuration and counter data distribution. Engine instances are scaled based on concurrent tenant processing needs, with each instance managing up to 10,000 tenants to maintain <5ms p99 latency target.
blueprint.reliability: The system achieves 99.99% availability through: 1) Multi-instance RateLimitingEngine with automatic failover (health checks every 100ms), 2) Redis cluster with master-slave replication for TenantConfigStore and counter storage, 3) Stateless APIGateway nodes with no local storage, 4) Optimized HTTP/2 connection pooling from gateways to engines for real-time decision streaming, 5) Circuit breaker pattern in engine instances to detect Redis unavailability and gracefully degrade, 6) Local in-memory cache layer that temporarily stores tenant configurations during Redis outages.
blueprint.disaster_recovery: For disaster recovery, the system implements: 1) Redis cluster with master-slave replication across availability zones, 2) Multi-region failover capability for RateLimitingEngine instances using Kubernetes deployment strategies, 3) Real-time replication of configuration changes to multiple Redis nodes with <1 minute RPO, 4) Hot standby Redis cluster with automatic failover within <30 seconds, 5) Data replication across multiple Redis nodes to prevent single points of failure in counter storage.
blueprint.observability: The system includes: 1) Real-time metrics collection for rate-limit decisions (latency, throughput, success/failure rates), 2) Distributed tracing using OpenTelemetry for end-to-end request flow tracking, 3) Prometheus metrics exposed by all components with Grafana dashboards, 4) Alerting thresholds set at 5ms p99 latency and 0.01% error rate, 5) Centralized logging via ELK stack with structured logs from all services, 6) Dedicated Prometheus metrics to track atomic counter operations and detect anomalies such as failed atomic claims or counter increment failures.
failure_scenarios: RateLimitingEngine instance fails: Automatic failover within 100ms through health checks; Redis cluster maintains counter state; API gateways reconnect to new engine instance without interrupting service

TenantConfigStore Redis cluster node fails: Master-slave replication ensures no data loss; Engine instances continue processing with cached configurations until recovery; Configuration updates are retried once restored

RateLimitingEngine Redis cluster failure: Counter state is maintained in memory for 60 seconds (window size) to prevent immediate service disruption; System continues operating with eventual consistency model

APIGateway node loses connection to RateLimitingEngine: Optimized HTTP/2 connection pooling with automatic reconnection mechanism; Gateways cache recent tenant configurations for up to 1 minute during disconnection
High-concurrency race condition in counter increment: Lock-free atomic operations prevent contention; System handles over 500,000 requests/sec without counter corruption or enforcement errors
Tenant configuration update conflict: Optimistic locking with retry logic ensures consistency; No data loss or inconsistency during high-volume configuration changes
Redis unavailability: Circuit breaker pattern detects Redis failure and gracefully degrades by allowing all requests through with warning logs; Local cache maintains operations for up to 5 minutes

decisions.decision: Use atomic counters with lock-free operations for rate limiting
decisions.alternatives_considered: Probabilistic data structures (Count-Min Sketch), sliding window with atomic counters, fixed window, token bucket, leaky bucket algorithms
decisions.trade_offs: Atomic operations provide strong consistency but require more compute resources; probabilistic structures offer better scalability but introduce small false positive rates.
decisions.rationale: Required under 5ms p99 latency for rate-limit decisions. Atomic operations ensure correctness under 500K requests/sec load, eliminating the need for fallback validation on every request.

decisions.decision: Implement optimistic locking with retry logic for configuration updates
decisions.alternatives_considered: Queue-based system, optimistic locking with retry logic, pessimistic locking, single writer per tenant, distributed consensus protocols
decisions.trade_offs: Optimistic locking provides better performance under moderate load but may cause retries during high-concurrency scenarios.
decisions.rationale: Configuration updates are infrequent compared to request volume but could be substantial during peak usage. Optimistic locking with retry logic balances performance and consistency.

decisions.decision: Use fixed consistent hashing with virtual nodes for tenant distribution
decisions.alternatives_considered: Adaptive sharding based on load metrics, static consistent hashing, round-robin, random distribution, fixed sharding
decisions.trade_offs: Fixed consistent hashing provides better distribution and prevents hotspots but requires more complex node management; adaptive sharding is simpler but causes hotspots.
decisions.rationale: Required to avoid hotspots in high-traffic scenarios where tenant request volumes are unevenly distributed. Fixed consistent hashing with virtual nodes ensures efficient resource utilization without operational complexity.

decisions.decision: Use optimized HTTP/2 connection pooling for engine decisions
decisions.alternatives_considered: Persistent WebSocket connections, REST endpoints, gRPC streaming with buffering, message queues, event-driven architecture
decisions.trade_offs: HTTP/2 provides low-latency, efficient communication with connection pooling but requires careful management of concurrent connections.
decisions.rationale: Required to maintain under 5ms p99 rate-limit decision latency while avoiding the overhead of gRPC streaming that would exceed the latency budget.

decisions.decision: Implement circuit breaker and local caching for Redis unavailability
decisions.alternatives_considered: Simple retry logic, full failover, graceful degradation, complete service interruption
decisions.trade_offs: Circuit breaker adds complexity but provides better resilience; simple retry may cause cascading failures.
decisions.rationale: Ensures continued operation during Redis outages by allowing all requests through with warning logs and maintaining local cache for up to 5 minutes.
